title: Python Strings
relevance: String creation, indexing, slicing, immutability, and common methods are staple Python OA and campus SDE fundamentals checks.

phases.goal: Establish what a Python string is and how to create one correctly.

must_hit.point: A Python string is a sequence of Unicode characters used to represent text.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says string = sequence of characters, and in Python specifically Unicode characters.

must_hit.point: The same string can be built with single quotes, double quotes, triple single quotes, triple double quotes, or the str() constructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those five interchangeable creation forms.

must_hit.point: Choosing the other quote style lets a quote character appear literally inside the text without escaping.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives an example like double quotes around text containing an apostrophe.

probes: What is a string in Python, and what are the ways you can create one?

hints.1: Think about characters and how quotes relate to text.
hints.2: Python strings are Unicode sequences; creation covers quote styles and str().
hints.3: A string is a sequence of Unicode characters; build it with ', ", ''', """, or str(), and pick the other quote style to embed a quote literally.

phases.goal: Check indexing, slicing rules, immutability, deletion, and core string operations.

must_hit.point: Positive indexing counts from the left starting at 0; negative indexing counts from the right starting at -1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both directions and their start values; may mention s[-1] is the last character.

must_hit.point: A slice uses s[start:stop:step]: start is included, stop is excluded, step defaults to 1, and any of the three may be omitted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the form and included/excluded/default rules.

must_hit.point: With a positive step you need start < stop; with a negative step you need start > stop; mismatched direction yields an empty string rather than an error.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains direction constraints and empty-string outcome on mismatch.

must_hit.point: Omitting both endpoints with step -1 reverses the whole string — the idiomatic Python reversal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names s[::-1] as reverse.

must_hit.point: Strings are immutable: assigning to an index raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment; change by building a new string and rebinding.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names immutability, the TypeError, and rebuild-via-slice/concat approach.

must_hit.point: del deletes a name binding entirely; deleting a slice fails with TypeError: 'str' object does not support item deletion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts del s vs del of a slice and the TypeError.

must_hit.point: + concatenates strings and * repeats a string; relational operators compare strings lexicographically by Unicode values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions +/* and lexicographic/Unicode comparison.

must_hit.point: An empty string is falsy and a non-empty string is truthy; and returns the second operand if the first is truthy, or returns the first if it is truthy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States emptiness truthiness and and/or return-operand behavior.

probes: How do indexing and slicing work on strings, and what happens if you try to change a character in place?

hints.1: Recall left/right indices and that strings cannot be edited by index.
hints.2: Cover start:stop:step, direction rules, immutability TypeError, and +/* / comparisons.
hints.3: 0/-1 indexing; inclusive start exclusive stop; mismatched step direction → empty; s[::-1] reverses; s[0]='H' → TypeError; del name ok, del slice → TypeError; + concat, * repeat, lex compare.

phases.goal: Contrast lookup methods and casing/search helpers candidates must choose correctly.

must_hit.point: find returns the lowest index of a substring or -1 if not found; index is like find but raises ValueError when the substring is not found.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both return behaviors, including -1 vs ValueError.

must_hit.point: count returns the number of non-overlapping occurrences; startswith/endswith return booleans for prefix/suffix checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates count from boolean start/end checks.

must_hit.point: Membership with in / not in is case-sensitive.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly says case-sensitive membership.

probes: When would you use find versus index to look up a substring?

hints.1: Both locate a substring, but they differ when it is missing.
hints.2: One returns a sentinel index; the other raises.
hints.3: find → lowest index or -1; index → same but ValueError if missing; also note case-sensitive in/not in.

phases.goal: Apply common built-ins and methods to real string tasks.

must_hit.point: len returns character count; max/min return characters with highest/lowest Unicode value; sorted returns a list of characters sorted by Unicode values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names len, max, min, sorted and what each returns.

must_hit.point: Casing methods capitalize, title, upper, lower, and swapcase return a new string with modified casing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those methods and that they return new strings.

must_hit.point: format inserts values into placeholders, and index numbers like {0} control argument placement.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes format() and numbered placeholders.

must_hit.point: split splits into a list (default separator whitespace); join concatenates an iterable using the string as separator; replace substitutes a phrase; strip removes leading and trailing whitespace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers split, join, replace, and strip roles.

must_hit.point: Validation methods include isalnum, isalpha, isdigit, and isidentifier.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names those four checks.

must_hit.point: Strings are iterable, so you can loop character by character.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says for-loop over a string walks characters.

probes: Which built-ins and methods would you use to measure, case-change, split/join, and validate a string?

hints.1: Think length, casing, splitting, and checks like isdigit.
hints.2: Group len/max/min/sorted, casing methods, split/join/replace/strip, and is* validators.
hints.3: len/max/min/sorted; capitalize/title/upper/lower/swapcase; format; split/join/replace/strip; isalnum/isalpha/isdigit/isidentifier; for char in s.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both locate the lowest index of a substring; find returns -1 when missing, while index raises ValueError: substring not found — choose find when absence is normal, index when missing should be exceptional.

tradeoffs.topic: Editing by index vs rebuild and rebind
tradeoffs.strong_answer: In-place index assignment is impossible because strings are immutable (TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment); to change text, build a new string via slicing/concatenation and rebind the name.
Use the other outer quote style so an apostrophe or quote can appear literally without escaping, e.g. double quotes around text containing it's.

gotchas.trap: Indexing past the end of a string
gotchas.correction: Raises IndexError: string index out of range; there is no off-the-end sentinel — the position must exist.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a Jupyter/Colab cell's displayed output after editing code
gotchas.correction: Editing does not refresh shown output until re-execution; a stale prior result (e.g. from s[2:]) can disagree with current code like s[:3], which is hel — never trust a result you have not just run.

gotchas.trap: Assigning to a character by index, e.g. s[0] = 'H'
gotchas.correction: Strings are immutable; that raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment — rebuild and rebind instead.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a slice of a string with del
gotchas.correction: Fails with TypeError: 'str' object does not support item deletion; del only removes the whole name binding.

gotchas.trap: Mismatched slice direction (positive step with start > stop, or negative step with start < stop)
gotchas.correction: Yields an empty string rather than an error; read the slice as from start up to but not including stop stepping by step.
in and not in are case-sensitive.
